title: Service without an audience
hookLine: seva is service done with no reward in mind, and it is meant to change the one who serves

cards: A snowy street at six in the morning. One neighbor's walk is already shoveled. Nobody saw who did it.
Nobody ever will. Now, the last time you did something good for someone, did you tell anyone? A post, a mention at dinner, a little hint so they'd know it was you?

That pull is human. A kindness can feel half finished until someone sees it. Welcome to camp three: after seventy-five days of stories, the practices, one at a time, starting with the one Sikhs put first.

teach.b: Nishkam seva. Seva you already know from day one: service. Nishkam means without desire: nish, without; kam, wanting.
Service with nothing wanted back. No thanks, no credit, no reward, not even the good feeling of being seen as a good person. The Gurus put it at the heart of Sikh life.
In the Sukhmani, the long hymn of peace by Guru Arjan, a line says, in paraphrase, that whoever serves without desire for reward reaches the Lord.
And Guru Nanak says it from the other side: serve in this world, and you will find a seat in the court of the divine. Here's the surprising part. Seva isn't mainly about the person you help.
Of course they matter; the hungry get fed.

teach.h: SEVA CHANGES THE ONE WHO SERVES.
teach.b: But the Gurus say seva works on the one who serves. Sikhs say each good thing left unseen starves a little of the self that wants attention. Sikhs call that self haumai, and it gets a whole day later this week.
So seva is practice, like a scale on a piano: it's how the teaching gets out of your head and into your hands. That's why it opens camp three.
In the gurdwara you'll see it everywhere: people chopping onions, wiping tables, washing pots, and nobody announces who they are.
A doctor, a student, a grandmother, all with their sleeves rolled up.
The rule is simple. Do the good thing. Then walk away.

how: In gurdwaras, Sikhs of every background do seva side by side, cooking, cleaning and serving, and many try to do it quietly, without asking for thanks or recognition.

o: service done only in the gurdwara kitchen
service done with nothing wanted in return
service given as a debt owed to the Guru

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.

s: seva is mainly about the people you help
they matter, but the Gurus say seva works on the one who serves, thinning the self that wants attention.
nish, without; kam, wanting: service with nothing wanted back.
in the gurdwara, important people are excused from seva
a doctor, a student and a grandmother all roll up their sleeves.

games.q: you've just shoveled your neighbor's walk before dawn. at breakfast they mention a mystery helper. what does nishkam seva suggest you do?
o: tell them it was you, so they can thank you.
drop a hint and let them guess.
games.why: nishkam seva is service with nothing wanted back, not even thanks. the Gurus say that's where it does its work.

practice: Think of one small, unseen kindness you could do, like refilling the coffee filter at work, taking a neighbor's bin in, or paying a small bill someone won't notice.
Picture doing it and walking away without a word, and notice the little itch to be known. You don't have to fight it; just see it, and smile at it.

wordCard.voice: Nishkam seva. Selfless service: help given with nothing wanted back, which changes the one who gives it.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: service without desire for reward.

carryVoice: Your line: no one needs to know. The good gets done either way. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 286 (Sukhmani, Guru Arjan: one who serves without desire for reward reaches the Lord)
Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 26 (Guru Nanak, Sri Raag: serve in this world and find a seat in the divine court)
